name: Nora Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, 27, and I lead a small electrical crew doing shops and home repairs. My two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence get me the awkward faults, but this small firm's pay is low and I've less than a month's expenses saved. I live alone, and there aren't many other electrical firms near me. I use AI daily to tidy my job notes, then spend most of the day testing circuits and finding why something won't stay on; finding the fault is lovely, chasing overdue wages isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quieter technology story doesn't mean we can forget wages. My boss still needs to pay on the date written on our slips. I can enjoy a useful note-writing tool without pretending the whole trade has changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already watching the bank balance more than the AI news. A late wage would eat almost all my spare cash, and the few nearby firms aren't advertising. My daily AI helper saves minutes at the desk, not my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'll put 20 from every weekly wage into a separate rent reserve, when the wage actually arrives. During the next year I'd keep leading the same testing and repair jobs. I won't buy a new tablet just because the software looks clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money even in this quieter picture. I like being useful on site, but a completed job doesn't become food until the wage clears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time your wage was late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Friday I checked my balance in the van before buying groceries. The wage arrived that afternoon, but I put the basket back once before it did. That's the ordinary worry I'm bringing into your question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a colleague who thinks your AI interest means you support everything management does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleague Sana that liking AI doesn't make late pay acceptable. I'd ask our crew to raise wage dates together at the next staff meeting. I favour a union, though I haven't joined one yet.

say: I'd tell the crew **wage dates** still matter when the technology news becomes quieter.
I can value a **useful tool** without claiming our whole trade has changed.
think: I'm already anxious about **late pay**, with too little cash to absorb another delay.
My daily **AI helper** saves desk time, but nearby employers aren't offering another job.
do: Save **20 weekly** toward rent when wages arrive, starting this month.
Keep leading **testing and repairs** during the coming year.
Raise **wage dates** together with the crew at the next staff meeting.
feel: **Money anxiety** survives the quieter technology story, despite satisfaction in solving faults.
S0.quote: My daily AI helper saves minutes at the desk, not my rent.
fieldNote: Her **bank balance** makes the baseline anxious; the concern predates any large technology change.
She separates daily **AI use** from accepting poor treatment and proposes a specific shared wage discussion.

steps.text: Save 20 from each paid weekly wage toward rent
Keep leading electrical testing and repair jobs
Raise wage dates together at the crew meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that quoting and booking are changing before anyone climbs into a ceiling. We should ask where the saved time goes. I'd rather share shorter paperwork than quietly squeeze the office worker out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my paid day is still hands and meters, so I don't expect my job to vanish now. I do think my hours could shrink if cheaper quotes push prices down. My boss already asks how fast we can finish, not just whether the circuit is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask to spend one paid hour a week learning the firm's AI quoting tool alongside our office worker. In the first year I'd compare ten machine estimates with actual site time and bring the errors to our crew meeting. I'd keep the weekly rent saving from the quieter picture when I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I can see work I can do about it. An estimate that misses a locked ceiling hatch becomes my unpaid evening if nobody challenges it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when a quick estimate misses a real obstacle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down the extra access time on the same job sheet as the estimate. I wouldn't agree that a cheap quote makes safe testing optional. My master licence is a responsibility, not a speed badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your boss refuses the paid learning hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the boss won't give a paid hour, I'll use the free practice version for twenty minutes at home twice a week. I won't spend my rent reserve on the subscription. I'd still take those ten comparisons to the crew meeting.

say: I'd ask who receives the **saved time** before celebrating faster office work.
I'd tell colleagues that **booking and quoting** change before our hands-on wiring does.
think: I expect my **hands-on job** to remain, but price pressure could reduce my paid hours.
I'm worried that **unsafe speed** becomes the hidden price of a cheap estimate.
do: Learn **AI quoting** for a paid weekly hour, or use free home practice if refused.
Compare **ten estimates** with actual site time during the first year.
Continue the **rent reserve** when wages allow.
feel: **Anxious but purposeful**, with a concrete way to challenge unrealistic estimates.
S1.quote: My master licence is a responsibility, not a speed badge.
fieldNote: Her **technical standing** gives her evidence to question estimates, but doesn't protect her from lost hours.
The learning plan preserves the **paid-time condition** and a free alternative; rent money never funds software.

steps.text: Practise AI quoting weekly, using free home access if unpaid
Save 20 weekly toward rent when wages allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2028 changes the planning desk before 2031 changes the hands doing the wiring. We should bargain about the years in between. I'd ask for a joint meeting, not just a demonstration of the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 I expect office work to be squeezed hard, but I'd still have electrical repairs. Around 2031, if capable robots are available, I expect to lose a big part of my paid hours unless I find another role. A licence and three weeks of money aren't enough protection, and that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd contact the electrical workers' association with two colleagues and ask for a meeting about paid transition training. In 2029, the first year after thinking AGI arrives, I'd apply for a fault-diagnosis course only if fees and one workday a week are funded without cutting my wage. I'd keep building the rent reserve while I'm working; I can't finance a promise out of food money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed when I get to 2031, even though I'm excited by what the machines can do. I can imagine a perfect repair being sold for less than my travel time. I don't have a second income to lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you call if your hours disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my sister and say I may need a spare room if the hours disappear, but I wouldn't count a yes before asking. Right now I'd stay in my flat and keep paying rent. Asking isn't a move or a guaranteed rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your enthusiasm for AI fit with asking colleagues to organise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still use the AI tools because avoiding them doesn't lengthen the runway. The uncomfortable part is organising with people who think my enthusiasm helped bring this on. I can want better tools and still want the people paid.

say: I'd tell the crew **2028 planning** and later robot work need different preparations.
I'd ask colleagues to **bargain together** about paid transition training.
think: I expect to lose a **large income share** around 2031 unless I secure another role.
My **thin reserve** cannot fund the gap, despite useful repair work before robots arrive.
do: Contact the **workers' association** now with two colleagues about paid transition training.
Apply for **fault-diagnosis training** in 2029 only with funded fees and one paid workday weekly, without cutting wages.
Keep adding to the **rent reserve** while wages permit.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless** about later lost hours, while still curious about the machines.
S2.quote: I can't finance a promise out of food money.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **2028 thinking work** from the expected income loss when capable robots follow around 2031.
Her course application depends on **funded fees** and maintained wages, rather than presumed support or a guaranteed new job.

steps.text: Ask the workers’ association for paid transition training with colleagues
Apply for 2029 diagnosis training only with funded fees and paid weekly study day maintaining wages
Build the rent reserve while electrical wages permit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to negotiate something real. I'd still name the later robot date, around 2034, because the planning software isn't the whole electrician's job. I wouldn't promise anybody a safe new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with the fast picture, I could finish some training before the office work changes. My own income could still shrink, especially when robots follow, but I don't think the loss is already decided. I have time to test another role while this wage still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd enrol in a free evening course on checking building energy use; the centre has offered the class, not a job. I'd keep my electrical shifts and save 20 weekly when paid. During 2032 I'd apply for posted building-maintenance roles that combine site checks with electrical fault work, accepting only an offer that covers my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, though I can sleep better than in the two-year picture. A real class on Tuesday gives the worry an address. The extra years matter because I don't have money to buy a year off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually practise in that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry my meter and do the readings myself, then compare the report with the class tutor. I'm learning how to check a building, not assuming reports will escape thinking AI. Physical checks might also change later, so I'd keep testing demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to leave your present firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the employer for the wage and hours in writing before resigning. Some similar jobs near me doesn't suddenly become true because I've taken a class. I'd search the actual vacancies and stay put if none pays enough.

say: I'd say **five years** makes a negotiated transition more practical, without guaranteeing another job.
I'd remind colleagues that capable **robots follow** thinking AGI around 2034.
think: I could test another role **before 2031** while still earning my electrical wage.
My income could still shrink, but I don't regard the **loss as settled**.
do: Enrol this winter in the **free evening course** on checking building energy use.
Save **20 weekly** when paid while keeping electrical shifts.
Apply in **2032** for posted maintenance jobs, moving only for rent-covering written terms.
feel: **Anxious with more control**, because learning can happen alongside paid work.
S3.quote: A real class on Tuesday gives the worry an address.
fieldNote: The longer runway changes **training feasibility**, not her assumptions about which occupations stay safe.
She ties any **job change** to an actual vacancy and written pay; local opportunities remain scarce.

steps.text: Attend the free evening building energy-checking course this winter
Save 20 weekly while keeping electrical shifts
Apply for posted maintenance roles in 2032 with rent-covering written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends I won't spend ten years rehearsing a disaster every morning. I'd like the crew to win training time while we still have work. The point of a longer warning is to use ordinary weeks well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'll be 37, still needing many years of income. I'd have room to build skills and savings, but no reason to call myself safe when robots follow around 2039. I could still lose hours in the next few years if firms start preparing early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take that free energy-checking course now and keep the weekly 20 transfer. Each autumn I'd review actual building-maintenance vacancies rather than buying another course automatically. In 2037 I'd apply for any suitable posted role with written pay covering rent; if there isn't one, I'd continue repairs while reassessing robot orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but the worry no longer fills every evening. Ten years can hold a lot of ordinary paydays. I'd like some of those paydays to leave money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you protect outside work during that long preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep one evening a week for my friends and not turn every conversation into a prediction. I live alone, and a plan that's only work and courses would wear me down. That isn't giving up on preparing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would make you change your timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm each year what equipment it's actually ordered and what hours it expects to need. A glossy robot video wouldn't make me resign. An order and fewer booked shifts would make me bring the job search forward.

say: I'd say a **longer warning** should produce useful ordinary weeks, not constant rehearsals of disaster.
I'd ask the crew to seek **training time** while paid electrical work remains.
think: I'll still need decades of **income at 37**, so the long date doesn't remove the problem.
Early company preparations could reduce my **hours** before capable robots arrive around 2039.
do: Take the **free course** now; continue paid repairs if no suitable role exists in 2037, reassessing robot orders.
Maintain the **weekly 20** saving when wages arrive.
Review vacancies annually and apply in **2037** only for suitable written, rent-covering offers.
feel: **Anxious but less consumed**, with time left for friends alongside practical preparation.
S4.quote: Ten years can hold a lot of ordinary paydays.
fieldNote: At **37 in 2036**, she cannot treat the late scenario as retirement protection.
Her annual checks concern **actual orders** and hours, keeping speculation from becoming an unsupported immediate exit.

steps.text: Take the free energy-checking course while retaining electrical shifts
Save 20 weekly when wages arrive over the preparation period
Seek suitable posted maintenance work in 2037 with rent-covering written terms
Continue paid repairs and reassess robot orders if no suitable posted role exists in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my hours to fall hard once robots follow, before I've built a proper reserve. Paid training with fees covered and wages kept whole would help, and a crew that can negotiate together would make the offer less one-sided. I need a bridge made of paid days, not a list of courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I enjoy being the person called when the fault makes no sense. I do, very much, and I want room for that pride alongside the money worry. Liking my work doesn't mean I can afford to lose the wage.

headlineQuote: I need a bridge made of paid days, not a list of courses.
portrait: At **27**, Nora leads electrical work with a technical diploma and master licence, but low pay leaves under one month's expenses.
She lives **alone**, uses AI daily, and values difficult fault-finding despite late wages and scarce nearby alternatives.
Her **progressive outlook** turns private money worry into shared requests for wage reliability and paid training.
Faster change leaves her **alarmed**; longer warnings allow free study and conditional job searches without pretending another occupation stays safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little time to build reserves before expected sharp hour losses when robots follow.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** must cover fees and preserve wages, with colleagues able to negotiate the terms together.
